title: Origen's search
hookLine: a brilliant, controversial teacher who read scripture as a journey upward

lines: EVENING AND MORNING, THE FIRST DAY.
cards: Read the first chapter of Genesis slowly and something odd turns up. "And the evening and the morning were the first day." Then a second day.
Then a third. Evenings and mornings, one after another. And only on the fourth day does God make the sun.
In Alexandria, a teacher named Origen noticed exactly this, and pointed it out to his readers. He didn't close the book. He didn't pretend not to see it.
He took it as a signal: keep going, there's more here than the surface.

teach.b: Origen gave his students a picture. A human being, he said, is body, soul and spirit, and so is scripture. Paul uses those three words together: "your whole spirit and soul and body."

The body of scripture is its plain sense, the story as it stands, and Origen held that it feeds many readers well. The soul is what the text asks of your life. The spirit is where it points: toward Christ and toward God.
So reading becomes a climb, from the words, through your life, up toward God.

teach.h: THE LETTER KILLETH, THE SPIRIT GIVETH LIFE.
teach.b: He leaned on Paul again: "the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life."
He was brilliant, and he was controversial, then and later. Some of his bolder guesses, about where souls come from and how all things end, were condemned long after he died.
Others honor him as a giant of Christian learning. Christians still argue about how to read him, and this path won't settle it. Tradition says he suffered in a persecution for his faith.
Here's his search on the road. In Luke, two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger who opens the scriptures to them. Only later do they recognize the risen Jesus.
Afterward they say: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" That's reading upward. And look back at this week's road.
A friend as the third in the room. Thanks in every thing. A holy laugh.
Love gathering up the law. Seeds of truth. Matter that matters.
And now a search that keeps climbing.

how: Christians read scripture for its plain sense and for deeper meanings; spiritual reading such as lectio divina moves slowly from what a text says to what it asks and to prayer, and preachers draw out both history and meaning.

o: a hunt for the oldest surviving copies of the Gospels
reading scripture as a climb from words up toward God
a quest to find where the Garden of Eden once stood

p: what it asks of your life

s: Origen ignored the plain sense of scripture
he called the plain sense scripture's body and held that it feeds many readers. he read upward from it.
in Genesis 1, evenings and mornings come before the sun is made
the sun is made on the fourth day; Origen pointed this out as a reason to read deeper.
Origen's ideas have never been argued over
some of his bolder guesses were condemned long after he died; others honor him as a giant of Christian learning.

games.q: you're reading Genesis 1 and notice evenings and mornings before the sun exists. what do you do?
o: close the book. it can't be right.
keep reading, and look for a deeper sense.
games.why: Origen pointed out the puzzle himself and took it as a signal to read for a spiritual meaning, climbing from the letter toward God.

practice: Take one line from the Psalms, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want," and give each layer a few breaths: what does it say, a shepherd, a sheep, enough; what does it ask of your life today, maybe to stop grabbing; and where does it point?
Let it lead you upward as far as it will go, and if you pray, rest in the line itself.

wordCard.voice: Origen's search. A teacher who read scripture as a climb, from its plain sense, through the life of the reader, up toward God.

carryVoice: Your line: read upward. From the words, through your life, up toward God. That closes the week.
